Below is a generic, software-agnostic workflow for altering or “retouching” a digital image. You can map these steps onto virtually any modern image-editing package (e.g. Adobe Photoshop, GIMP, Affinity Photo, Lightroom, Capture One) or even specialized AI-assisted tools.

1. Preparation and Planning  
  • Define your visual goal (e.g. change color balance, remove unwanted elements, composite new objects).  
  • Gather all source materials—high-resolution originals, any reference images, textures, or masks you may need.  
  • (Optional) Calibrate your display and set up a consistent color space (e.g. sRGB or Adobe RGB) so edits look predictable.

2. Importing and Organization  
  • Open your image in the editor or import it into a cataloging module.  
  • Create a project folder structure: Originals, Exports, Textures, Masks, Assets.  
  • Duplicate the base layer or use a non-destructive workflow (e.g. adjustment layers, layer comps).

3. Basic Corrections  
  • Crop and straighten: remove unwanted borders or realign the horizon.  
  • Exposure and contrast: use Levels or Curves adjustments to set proper black-point, midtones, and highlights.  
  • White balance and color cast: adjust temperature/tint or use color-balance sliders.  
  • Lens corrections (distortion, vignetting) if needed.

4. Precise Selections and Layering  
  • Use marquee, lasso, or pen-tool selections to isolate regions (foreground, sky, subjects).  
  • Refine edges with feathering, edge-detection brushes, or “select and mask” routines.  
  • Place isolated elements on separate layers so you can manipulate them individually.

5. Retouching and Cleanup  
  • Healing/Spot-healing Brush and Clone Stamp: remove blemishes, sensor dust spots, stray objects.  
  • Patch or Content-Aware Fill: replace large unwanted areas by sampling surrounding textures.  
  • Frequency separation (in portrait retouching): split fine texture from color/tone for independent correction.

6. Color and Tone Enhancement  
  • Adjustment layers (Curves, Levels, Exposure) for global tone.  
  • Hue/Saturation or Selective Color to tweak specific color ranges.  
  • Gradient Maps or Lookup Tables (LUTs) for stylized color grading.  
  • Dodge & Burn: lighten or darken local areas to guide the eye and add depth.

7. Transformations and Warping  
  • Scale, rotate, skew, or perspective-correct individual layers.  
  • Liquify or warp tools to subtly reshape forms (e.g. facial features, fabrics).  
  • Puppet-warp or mesh-based warping for more controlled distortions.

8. Blending and Compositing (if adding new elements)  
  • Layer blend modes (Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Soft Light, etc.) to integrate textures or sky replacements.  
  • Masks: paint in or erase parts of layers with a soft brush for smooth transitions.  
  • Match lighting and perspective: use shadow layers (soft-edged black shapes with reduced opacity) and dodge/burn to simulate consistent illumination.

9. Detail Work and Sharpening  
  • High-pass sharpening: apply a high-pass filter on a duplicate layer set to Overlay or Soft Light.  
  • Selective sharpening: mask noisy or out-of-focus areas to avoid accentuating artifacts.  
  • Noise reduction: apply denoise filters carefully to preserve detail.

10. Special Effects and Filters  
  • Film-style grain or texture overlays.  
  • Bokeh, lens flare, or glow effects using radial gradients and blend modes.  
  • Vignettes or edge-darkening to frame the subject.

11. Final Checks and Output  
  • Turn layers on/off to compare “before” and “after.”  
  • Inspect at 100% zoom for artifacts, halos, or banding.  
  • Flatten or export as layered source file (e.g. PSD, XCF) plus a separate flattened copy (JPEG, TIFF, PNG) at the desired resolution.  
  • Embed or convert to the target color profile for web, print, or display.

12. (Optional) Automation and Batch Processing  
  • Record macros or actions for repetitive tweaks (resizing, watermarking, basic color presets).  
  • Use scripts or watch-folders to apply consistent processing to large image sets.

13. Emerging AI-Assisted Techniques  
  • Inpainting/generative fill: select an area and let the model automatically generate matching content.  
  • AI-driven upscaling or super-resolution to boost detail.  
  • Style transfer or neural filters for rapid artistic reimaginings.

By following these stages—planning, basic correction, detailed retouch, compositing, final enhancement, and output—you can systematically modify virtually any digital image to achieve a wide array of visual outcomes.
